explanations.explanation: David says, "I bow down toward Your holy temple…" He sings AND he bows, so his whole self is thanking God. I think that's what happens when thanks gets too big to stay in your mouth. It spills into your knees.
Sinai never shows up in these eight verses. David names exactly one direction, and it's toward God's holy temple. Nice try, friend, but that's a long walk in the wrong direction for this psalm.

The Jordan River isn't in this psalm at all. David says, "I bow down toward Your holy temple…" So the direction is the temple, and the river can stay out of it. I'll admit it's a fun guess, though, and I've definitely faced the wrong way before. Usually toward the cooling rack.
David says it plain: "On the day I called, You answered me…" Notice he doesn't say God got back to him eventually. He says on the day. David is looking back and giving thanks for exactly that.

That word isn't in the verse. David says, "On the day I called, You answered me…" He also says God emboldened him and strengthened his soul. That's what he remembers from that day, and it's the opposite of being left hanging.
David says the opposite. "On the day I called, You answered me…" No voicemail, no waiting room. That's why he's singing with all his heart in the first place.
David doesn't stop at Israel's kings. He says, "All the kings of the earth will give You thanks, O LORD…" That's the whole earth, not one kingdom. The guest list got a lot bigger than you'd think.

David says, "All the kings of the earth will give You thanks, O LORD…" That's every king on earth, not only the ones from home. And he says it will happen when they hear the words of the LORD's mouth. Good catch, baker.

David says the kings will give thanks "when they hear the words of Your mouth." Hearing comes first, and then the thanks. I think that's how it goes for any of us. Somebody tells you the good news, and then you can't stop talking about it.
Doubt isn't in the verse. David says the kings give thanks "when they hear the words of Your mouth." Hearing is what sets the thanks off. Doubting would be a very different psalm.

Forgetting wouldn't lead to thanks, and David never says it. He says the kings give thanks "when they hear the words of Your mouth." So it's the hearing that matters. Forgetting is how I lose my oven mitts.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD's glory is great
explanations.explanation: David gives the reason right in the verse: "They will sing of the ways of the LORD, for the glory of the LORD is great." The kings sing because of who the LORD is. His glory is great, and that's reason enough.

David doesn't give the kings any orders in this psalm. He says they will sing "for the glory of the LORD is great." The reason is the LORD's glory, not anything David says. Nobody has to be bossed into singing about that.

No armies come up anywhere in these verses. David says, "They will sing of the ways of the LORD, for the glory of the LORD is great." The reason he gives is the LORD's glory, and that's the whole answer.

David says, "Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly…" High up and still paying attention to the lowly. That's the surprise in the verse, and it's good news for anybody who feels small. I've been small. I've been small in a drawer.

The verse goes the other way. David says, "Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly…" The word "though" is the clue, because it sets up a surprise. The surprise is that He looks at the lowly.

Fame doesn't come up in the verse. David says, "Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly…" No fan club needed to get His attention. Good news for those of us with a small following, friend.

explanations.answer: The LORD knows them from afar
explanations.explanation: David says, "…but the proud He knows from afar." The lowly get His attention, and the proud get Him from a distance. I'll leave it at what the verse says, and the verse says afar.

explanations.answer: The LORD lifts them up high
explanations.explanation: That's not what David says. The verse says, "…but the proud He knows from afar." So the proud aren't lifted up. They're known from a distance.

The verse puts it the other way. David says, "…but the proud He knows from afar." Afar means at a distance, not sitting next to them. Nobody gets a seat at the table by acting like they own the table.

David says, "If I walk in the midst of trouble, You preserve me from the anger of my foes…" Notice he's walking in the midst of trouble, not around it. And God preserves him right there. I think that's a pretty comforting picture.
There's no sea and no storm in this psalm. David says God preserves him "from the anger of my foes." So the trouble David pictures is people angry at him, not weather.
A famine isn't in these verses. David says, "If I walk in the midst of trouble, You preserve me from the anger of my foes…" The danger he names is his foes' anger. Not an empty pantry.

David says, "O LORD, Your loving devotion endures forever…" Forever means no expiration date and no best-by stamp. David has just said the LORD will fulfill His purpose for him, so he's ending on solid ground.

The text says the opposite. David says, "O LORD, Your loving devotion endures forever…" Forever, baker, not for a season. He prays that line right after saying the LORD will fulfill His purpose for him.

explanations.answer: That God not abandon what His hands made
explanations.explanation: David's last line is, "…do not abandon the works of Your hands." He ends with a request, and it comes right after saying the LORD's loving devotion endures forever. After all that confidence, he still asks. I think that says a lot about how close he feels to God.

explanations.answer: That God bring down the proud
explanations.explanation: David never asks for that. The proud come up in verse 6, where he says the LORD knows them from afar. His final request is, "…do not abandon the works of Your hands." His last line is about God holding on to what He made.

explanations.answer: That God make his name great
explanations.explanation: David asks nothing about his own name here. The name he lifts up is God's, since he says God has exalted His name and His word above all else. His final line is, "…do not abandon the works of Your hands." He's not angling for a bigger name, friend.
